content: Severe health consequences can occur in humans or animals exposed to certain biological agents. In this context, substances classified as Category A infectious substances are those known or reasonably expected to contain biological agents capable of causing severe disability, life-threatening conditions, or fatal illnesses in exposed individuals. Transport regulations and agreements often provide indicative lists of such agents, with an example list included in Annex 3 of this document. However, many agents on these lists only meet the criteria for Category A when transported as cultures. It is important to note that not all forms of an infectious substance are capable of causing infection, even if the same biological agent is present. For instance, Mycobacterium tuberculosis is only considered highly harmful when transported as a culture. The classification of infectious substances involves assigning them to specific UN numbers and proper shipping names. Infectious substances that can cause disease in humans or both humans and animals are assigned to UN 2814 with the shipping name INFECTIOUS SUBSTANCE, AFFECTING HUMANS. Substances that only affect animals are assigned to UN 2900 with the shipping name INFECTIOUS SUBSTANCE, AFFECTING ANIMALS ONLY. If the biological agent is known, its technical name must be included in parentheses after the shipping name on transport documents, though it is not required on the package itself. For example, UN 2814 may be labeled as Infectious substance affecting humans (Mycobacterium tuberculosis cultures). If the agent is unknown but suspected to meet Category A criteria, the term suspected Category A infectious substance must be used in parentheses after the shipping name. Accurate classification of infectious substances as Category A requires professional judgment, particularly for new or emerging pathogens that may not appear on indicative lists but share similar characteristics with known Category A agents. A pathogen risk assessment should consider medical histories, symptoms, endemic conditions, and the source of the substance. In cases of uncertainty, a cautious approach should be taken, and the substance should be classified as Category A. Medical or clinical waste containing Category A substances must be assigned to UN 2814, UN 2900, or UN 3549, as appropriate, with proper shipping names reflecting their contents and origin. For most infectious substances that do not meet the high-risk criteria of Category A, transport under Category B is sufficient. These are assigned to UN 3373 with the shipping name BIOLOGICAL SUBSTANCE, CATEGORY B. Medical or clinical waste containing Category B agents is assigned to UN 3291. This system includes a leakproof primary receptacle, a secondary container, and a rigid outer packaging layer. For air transport, specific quantity limits apply, such as a maximum of 1 liter per primary receptacle and 4 liters per outer package. These packages must be marked with the UN packaging symbol and other identifying information, including the year of manufacture and the competent authority that approved the packaging. Coolants, such as dry ice or liquid nitrogen, are often used to maintain the integrity of infectious substances during transport. Liquid nitrogen, classified as Dangerous Goods Class 2, requires packaging that can withstand extremely low temperatures. Specialized packaging, such as dry shippers, can safely contain liquid nitrogen without additional dangerous goods requirements. Stabilizers, such as sorbitol, fetal bovine serum, or alcohol solutions, may also be included with infectious substances to maintain viability or prevent degradation. If stabilizers are classified as dangerous goods, their transport must comply with relevant regulations.
